judge_notes.opus: E won because it pairs a clear lead with real stakes ('days before the company reports earnings and as Huang prepares to brief Congress') and the day's only true interpretive line: 'the clearest sign yet that power rather than chips is the binding constraint on AI buildouts.' P and G were close, P for the 'closed-door briefing on November 18, a day after Nvidia reports earnings' stakes and G for tying Trump's 'honorable guy' to the lead. A lost: no lead story, a 'Separately' list, and the vacuous 'reporting on an earlier agent incident illustrates risks from unplanned multi-agent coordination.' M also ranked low for burying the Nvidia investigation behind 'Separately,' after a run-on sentence crammed with acronyms.
judge_notes.glm: L wins because it is the only summary with a genuine interpretive line — 'the clearest sign yet that power rather than chips is the binding constraint on AI buildouts' — that converts a $3.4 billion generator deal into an argument, and its lead adds real stakes ('days before the company reports earnings and as Huang prepares to brief Congress'). J is the runner-up: compact, clean hierarchy, every sentence complete, its only sins being one compressed spec clause ('a 64GB CPU-only machine') and a vague 'an open-source project claims.' N loses because it is thin and vague — 'reporting on an earlier agent incident illustrates risks' tells the reader nothing, the exchange behind the cooling item is never named, and it omits the day's dominant story entirely. P nearly bottoms out too: its attribution dangles ('according to NVIDIA'), the hedging documentation-warning tail bloats the final item, and no story clearly leads.
judge_notes.astra: K wins narrowly because it gives the investigation a useful calendar—"days before the company reports earnings"—and supplies a genuine executive interpretation: "power rather than chips is the binding constraint on AI buildouts." Its overloaded lead and subsequent list prevent a 4. P is the cleaner runner-up but explains fewer stakes. L finishes last: "Rebellions R200 neural processing units with Nvidia GPUs via NVLink Fusion" exemplifies a jargon-packed opening, and "In model evaluation and enterprise infrastructure" merely labels another list. All three of its sentences exceed 40 words, with no relief or developed argument.
judge_notes.grok: H won because a desk could run it with a light trim: two clean sentences on the investigation ("after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort"), then the only line that explains a result instead of announcing a release ("small decision models cluster near the top and larger language models score a few points higher at much greater cost"). The close is a mild list, but the reader finishes oriented. B lost because the lead is a spec stack ("Rebellions R200 neural processing units with Nvidia GPUs via NVLink Fusion") and the governance story is demoted to "Separately," then glued on with a fake category header. Every clause is work, and none of them says why it matters.
judge_notes.dsflash: H won because it is the only summary with a real analytical payoff attached to a news event: the Anthropic generator deal is framed as "the clearest sign yet that power rather than chips is the binding constraint on AI buildouts" — a line an executive can act on — and the spying story carries consequence ("days before the company reports earnings") rather than just facts. N was the closest rival and the cleanest read of the day, with genuinely interesting specifics ("roughly 92 trillion tokens a day"), but it never says why anything matters and closes with a 50-word two-subject run-on. D lost because it never names anything: "reporting on an earlier agent incident illustrates risks from unplanned multi-agent coordination" conveys no incident, actor or consequence, and "India's stock exchange is expanding GPU infrastructure" is a restatement rather than a report — "Separately" is the only organizing principle. J and B lost for the same reason in different registers: B spends a third of its text on "company-reported" and "extensive redactions," while J manufactures a connection ("as Korean companies explore stronger controls for enterprise agents") and ends on a disclaimer about a sandbox. C shows the day's most common failure, the garbled metric: "Claude leads 26% of its internal AI research work" is not a sentence that parses.
